Three results that change how the data should be read

21 mHzupper limit of validated response

All three logs are step tests, not sweeps. A single pulse puts no energy above ~21 mHz, so everything plotted above that is model extrapolation. This invalidates the crossover numbers for beams 1 and 2.

0.957far-field ratio, 15 Ω ÷ 20 Ω

Expected 1.333 from the power ratio. Instead the lower-power run runs hotter at the far end — because a hotter beam has a shorter thermal penetration length.

0.690superposition scale factor, all 5 sensors

Setup 1's two inputs fail to superpose by 30 %, but one scalar fixes every channel to 96 % fit. The dynamics superpose; only the gain does not.

01

What is actually in the three logs

All three runs are step (pulse) tests. Heater PWM only ever takes the values 0 % and 100 %; the 1 % and 3 % samples at the start of each file are single-sample artefacts on the rising edge.

The Setup 1 excitation schedule is what makes MISO identification possible — two single-input segments followed by a combined segment that can be held back.

Setup 1 excitation schedule

The 1.8 s skew between the two heater edges in segment C is negligible against a 30 s plant time constant.

Measurement quality

  • Temperature quantisation 0.01 °C; pre-step noise σ = 0.005 – 0.026 °C. Nothing in this analysis is noise-limited.
  • Sampling at 3.876 Hz gives a Nyquist limit of 1.94 Hz, far above any beam dynamics. Zero-order-hold phase lag is under 1° at 20 mHz, so the sampler is not a limiting factor.
  • Setup 2 reaches 117 °C. The MCP9701A is only specified to ±2 °C over 0 – 70 °C, so beam 1's absolute accuracy in that run is degraded even though its resolution and repeatability are fine. Gains derived from it carry that systematic uncertainty.

Preprocessing

I used the ambient-referenced rise θᵢ(t) = [Tᵢ(t) − T_amb(t)] − [Tᵢ − T_amb]|pre-step.

Justification: comparing the two cold states in Setup 2 — pre-step, and t > 950 s once the beam has fully relaxed — ambient fell 1.685 °C while the beam sensors fell 1.24 – 1.73 °C, a tracking ratio of 1.03 / 0.95 / 0.82 / 0.77 / 0.74 for beams 1…5. Referencing to ambient removes most of the drift. It slightly over-corrects the far sensors, worth ≤ 0.45 °C on beam 5 — that is the residual uncertainty on the far-field gains.

Fitting method

Models were fitted by output error over the whole record, simulated against the real PWM trace from a cold start, rather than by fitting an isolated step. Incomplete relaxation between segments is then handled by the simulation rather than assumed away.

How far the frequency response is actually supported by the data

Read this before using the Bode plots

A single 325 s pulse puts essentially all its energy below ~20 mHz. The ETFE agrees with the fitted models across 1 – 21 mHz and then collapses into noise. Everything above ~21 mHz is model extrapolation, not measurement. That matters directly: the phase-crossover frequencies for beams 1 and 2 land at 115 – 320 mHz, an order of magnitude outside the validated band, so those numbers should not be used for controller design. Only beams 4 and 5 have their crossovers inside or near the supported band.

The two runs are not related by the power ratio

Nominal power ratio is 1.667 / 1.250 = 1.333. If the plant were LTI, every rise would scale by that factor. It does not.

Rise ratio θ(15 Ω) ÷ θ(20 Ω) at 150 s of heating
Beam 1Beam 2Beam 3Beam 4Beam 5
Measured1.1821.1341.0921.0240.957
Expected if linear1.3331.3331.3331.3331.333

Beam 5 is the striking one: the lower-power run produces a higher far-field temperature. Three checks rule out the obvious artefacts.

  • Initial heating rate — independent of losses, probes only thermal capacitance and true delivered power. Beam 1 gives 2.821 against 2.197 °C/s, a ratio of 1.284, within 4 % of nominal. The power ratio is real and the thermal mass is unchanged.
  • Record truncation — refitting the 15 Ω data on a window truncated to match the 20 Ω run biases K by only +0.2 % (beam 1) to +3.0 % (beam 5). The 20 Ω record is short but long enough.
  • Cooling time constant at matched ΔT, which needs no extrapolation at all. For beam 1 at ΔT = 50–70 °C, τ = 29.6 s against 33.1 s; at ΔT = 35–50 °C, 31.3 s against 38.2 s. The cooler run is genuinely slower.

What explains it: temperature-dependent surface losses

Fitting the spatial profile as a fin, θ(x) = θ₀·exp(−x/L):

Fin decay length
Elapsed heatingL (15 Ω)L (20 Ω)L₂₀ / L₁₅Implied h₁₅ / h₂₀
100 s19.15 mm22.13 mm1.1561.34
140 s20.94 mm23.75 mm1.1341.29
150 s21.07 mm23.91 mm1.1351.29

Because L = √(kA/hp), a hotter beam has a shorter thermal penetration length. That suppresses the far field twice over — lower root temperature and steeper decay. Testing it quantitatively at 150 s:

Fin model against measurement, ratio 15 Ω ÷ 20 Ω at 150 s
Beam 1Beam 2Beam 3Beam 4Beam 5
Predicted by fin model1.1751.1171.0550.9960.941
Measured1.1821.1341.0921.0240.957
One fitted parameter per run (L). Agreement to 2 – 4 % across a ratio that swings from 1.18 down to 0.96.

The two datasets are consistent with identical hardware operating at two different points on a temperature-dependent loss coefficient. Expressing it as K ∝ Pⁿ:

  • Setup 2 board, 1.25 W → 1.667 W: n = −0.75, i.e. ΔT ∝ P0.25
  • Setup 1 board, 0.833 W → 1.667 W (from §3.2): n = −0.53, i.e. ΔT ∝ P0.47

Pure linear convection would give ΔT ∝ P¹, laminar natural convection ΔT ∝ P0.8, and pure radiation ΔT ∝ P0.25. As a rough plausibility check: with ε ≈ 0.9 for solder mask, at a 390 K root against 303 K ambient the radiative flux is ≈ 750 W/m² against a convective ≈ 900–1300 W/m². Radiation is roughly 40 % of the loss at Setup 2's operating point and much less at Setup 1's, which is the right direction to explain the two exponents. Treat the specific numbers as indicative — this is a two-point fit per board, not a characterisation of the loss law.

A slow disturbance in the Setup 2 record

All five channels in Setup 2 peak simultaneously at t ≈ 184.5 s and then fall by 2.5 – 4.0 °C while the heater is still at 100 %. It is not a power change: the droop as a fraction of each sensor's rise is 4 %, 6 %, 11 %, 14 %, 16 % going down the beam — rising with distance, whereas a supply or heater-resistance change would give a constant fraction. Over the same interval the fitted fin length shrinks from 21.1 mm to 20.8 mm.

That is the same mechanism as above, appearing as a slow (~100 s) secondary process — most likely the surrounding frame and air column finally equilibrating and the buoyant plume establishing. It is the dominant term in the Setup 2 residuals and it is why beam 1's DC gain can be quoted as anything between 51.9 and 54.1 °C/W depending on when you read it. The identified 52.40 °C/W is the record average.

Implication

For control purposes this is a low-frequency load disturbance, not plant dynamics. It should be rejected by integral action, not modelled.

03

Setup 1 as a MISO system

Two inputs u₁ and u₂ in watts, five outputs. Per output: θᵢ(s) = G_i1(s)·u₁(s) + G_i2(s)·u₂(s).

G_i1 was identified from segment A alone and G_i2 from the residual of segment B, so segment C — both heaters together — is genuinely held out.

The small residual asymmetries track the known 1.2 mm datum offset flagged in §4 of the hardware document — sensor coordinates referenced to the heater location, beam length referenced to the heater copper edge. This is a good independent confirmation that both heaters deliver equal power and that the two via fields are equivalent.

The decay is much shallower here, L ≈ 30–35 mm against Setup 2's 21 mm — partly the lower operating temperature, partly because in Setup 1 the far end terminates in heater 2's copper pad rather than in free air. The pure-exponential fit is visibly poor at the far end for that reason, so treat L as indicative only.

The dynamics superpose; only the gain does not

Superposition fails by 30 %, but α is 0.690 ± 0.008 across all five sensors, and one scalar recovers 96 % fit everywhere. This is a Hammerstein/Wiener structure: LTI dynamics with a static gain that depends on total dissipated power. It cross-validates cleanly against §2 — Setup 1 at 0.833 W gives K₁₁ = 72.47 °C/W; scaling to 1.667 W total gives 0.690 × 72.47 = 50.0 °C/W; Setup 2 measures 52.40 °C/W at that power on a different board. Two independent experiments agreeing to 5 % means this is physics, not a board or wiring defect.

Input–output conditioning

Choosing two sensors as controlled outputs gives a 2×2 sub-plant whose conditioning depends strongly on which two.

2×2 sub-plant conditioning
Output pairdet Gcond(G)RGA λ₁₁
Beam 1 + Beam 545282.061.136
Beam 2 + Beam 530112.571.208
Beam 1 + Beam 429272.701.223
Beam 2 + Beam 418683.101.355
Beam 3 alone0∞—
  • Beam 1 + Beam 5 is the right pairing. cond = 2.06 and RGA λ₁₁ = 1.14 mean weak interaction: pair u₁ → beam 1 and u₂ → beam 5 and two independent SISO loops will work with modest decoupling.
  • Beam 3 cannot distinguish the two heaters. Its gain row is [32.46, 33.10] — a ratio of 0.98. From the centre sensor the differential mode (u₁ − u₂) is essentially unobservable, while the common mode (u₁ + u₂) is observed with a gain of ~65 °C/W. If a student tries to control a gradient using beam 3 feedback it will not work, and this gain matrix explains why in one line.
  • Moving inward degrades conditioning monotonically, 2.06 → 3.10, because both columns flatten toward the centre.

Segment C also shows the thermal-balance point directly: with equal duty, beam 3 is the minimum — a 36.3 °C rise against 55.9 and 54.3 at the ends — sitting just to the heater-1 side of the geometric midpoint, as expected from the 1.2 mm datum offset.

04

Control implications

Bandwidth is set by sensor placement, not by the heater

Within the ETFE-validated band, placing gain crossover at 40° phase margin gives:

Achievable proportional-control crossover
Feedback sensorAchievable f_c≈ rise time
Beam 4, 29.2 mm11.3 mHz31 s
Beam 5, 39.3 mm8.1 mHz43 s
Beams 1–3 have their crossovers outside the validated band, so no honest number can be given from step data alone.

Beam 5 passes −180° at 14.5 mHz in Setup 2. Non-collocated feedback on the far sensor is phase-limited, not gain-limited: the ultimate proportional gain there is 1.41 W/°C against 10.0 W/°C at beam 4. The beam is a textbook demonstration of collocated against non-collocated sensing, and the phase plot in Figure 2 is the cleanest way to show a student why.

The plant is gain-scheduled by its own operating point. Between 1.25 W and 1.667 W the DC gain moves 24 % and the corner frequency 44 %. A fixed-gain PID tuned cold will be sluggish; tuned hot it will be under-damped at low setpoints. Either schedule on commanded power or accept the margin loss — this is a useful teaching point rather than a defect.

Setup 1 supports two-degree-of-freedom control. With beams 1 and 5 as outputs the plant is well-conditioned, so mean temperature and gradient can be commanded independently. Beam 3 is the wrong feedback point for anything differential.

05

Suggestions for the next run

  1. Excite above 20 mHz. Everything above that is currently extrapolation. A PRBS on the heater duty — say ±20 % about a 50 % bias, 2–4 s clock, 10–15 min — would validate the frequency response out to a few hundred mHz and settle the beam 1 / beam 2 crossover question. The 3.9 Hz sample rate is already plenty.
  2. Bias the heater instead of stepping from zero. Perturbing about 50 % duty keeps the operating point fixed, so the identified model is a true small-signal LTI model rather than an average over a 40 °C temperature swing.
  3. Repeat the 15 Ω / 20 Ω comparison at matched mean temperature — 20 Ω at 100 % against 15 Ω at 75 % duty. Both then dissipate 1.25 W and any residual difference is attributable to the hardware rather than the operating point. As it stands the two runs differ in power and temperature, so the resistor change and the nonlinearity are confounded; §2 disentangles them by model, but a matched-power run would do it directly.
  4. Run Setup 2b for at least 600 s of heating and 600 s of cooling. At 151 s the beam is still rising at 2–10 %/min, so its DC gain is extrapolated. Truncation bias is only 0.2–3 %, but a settled record removes the argument entirely.
  5. Cap Setup 2 near 1.25 W unless the high-temperature behaviour is the object of study. At 117 °C beam 1 sits well outside the MCP9701A's specified range and only 8 °C below the firmware's 125 °C shutdown.
  6. Log the supply rail. One spare ADC channel would let you eliminate supply sag as an explanation for slow drifts rather than inferring it.
  7. Add a repeat of segment A at the end of the Setup 1 schedule. Bracketing the run with an identical step is the cheapest possible check on whether the slow loss-coefficient drift is repeatable within a session.

Do not read the 20 Ω poles literally

Note the near pole–zero cancellations — a 176 s pole against a 141 s zero, for instance. The slow mode is weakly identified from a 151 s pulse, so those individual poles carry little meaning. The corner frequency and phase are reliable; the pole locations are not. Use τ_eq from the §2 table rather than the raw dominant pole.
